name: Omar Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Cobb's Orchards, about a hundred and twenty acres of apples and pears, mostly for supermarkets and a bit for juice. In November the picking's done, so it's the cold store, grading fruit as it goes out, and starting the winter pruning. Pruning is cutting back the branches so the tree fruits well next year, and it's harder than it looks. I'm out with secateurs and a ladder from eight until about four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you done it, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This is my third winter. Before that I worked sixteen years at the juice factory in Marden, on the bottling line, until they moved production abroad. Mr Cobb used to sell us his fruit, so I knew him a little and asked. I'm still learning to prune, the head man Dennis follows behind me and fixes my cuts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like blossom time in April, the whole valley white and pink, you forget the money for a week. What wears me out is the picking season, with forty pickers to look after and the supermarket wanting everything yesterday. And the pay is low. Leila, my wife, cuts hair three days a week, and we get by, just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful thing and leave it at that. Mr Cobb's daughter uses it to write the emails to the buyers. It doesn't prune a tree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's fine, a small help. I've used it a few times, once to ask about a canker on the Conference pears, and it was half right. I'd keep using it a little, the way you'd use a neighbour who reads a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now. I'd ask Dennis to teach me grafting this winter, which is the next skill up. And I'd try to clear the last six hundred on the car loan before summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to fear in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it was half right about the canker. Which half?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It knew what canker was and how it spreads. It told me to cut it out in wet weather, which Dennis says is exactly wrong, you do it dry or you spread it. So now I check with Dennis first and the phone second.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Leila think of these tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She uses it for the salon bookings, it sends the reminder messages. She says the no-shows went down by half. So in our house it's already saved more money than it's cost.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and leave it there. Mr Cobb's daughter uses it for buyer emails, but it doesn't prune a tree.
S0.think: I think it's a small help. I've used it a few times and it was half right, so I check with Dennis first and the phone second.
S0.do: Asks Dennis to teach him grafting this winter. Tries to pay off the last six hundred on the car loan before summer.
S0.quote: So now I check with Dennis first and the phone second.
S0.fieldNote: Omar is measured and fair, weighing each thing before he answers. He uses AI now and then and has already learned to trust it only so far, from a real mistake about pear canker. His wife's salon has had a clear win from it, which shapes his calm view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the one hand it gives people time to adjust, on the other hand the young ones get squeezed. Both are true. I'd say it like that, I don't like taking sides too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slow is good for me. Pruning, grafting, judging fruit, that's years to learn, and a slow change gives me those years. I worry more that Cobb's stops taking on seasonal youngsters and the farm gets older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn grafting properly, ask Mr Cobb to put me on the spraying course next spring. Maybe start a small savings pot, twenty a week, in a separate account so I can't see it. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. It's manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said twenty a week in an account you can't see. Have you tried that before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice. Both times the washing machine or the car found it. Leila says the money knows where it's hidden. Third time lucky, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the youngsters you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every summer we get students and local kids for picking, sixteen, seventeen. Some of them stay on, Dennis started as one. If those jobs dry up, there's no next Dennis.

S1.say: I'd say it gives people time to adjust but squeezes the young ones, and both are true. I don't like taking sides too fast.
S1.think: Slow change suits me, because pruning and grafting take years to learn. I worry more that Cobb's stops taking on young seasonal pickers and the farm gets older.
S1.do: Learns grafting and asks to join the spraying course next spring. Tries again to save twenty a week in a separate account.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but it feels manageable.
S1.quote: Leila says the money knows where it's hidden.
S1.fieldNote: He keeps both sides of every argument in view, which fits his centre outlook. He's realistic about saving: two earlier tries failed and he can laugh about it. His concern for future pickers came from the fact that the head man started as one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the politicians should stop shouting and do something sensible, like help with retraining. Some people would lose out, some would do well, it needs managing. I might share a news article, nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's a bigger worry for the buyers' side than for me. The supermarket buyers who haggle with Mr Cobb could be computers, and computers might be harder to haggle with. That would squeeze the price, and the price squeezes us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Cobb, straight, how the fruit price looks for next year. If it's falling, I'd look for a second job in winter, maybe evening shifts at the warehouse in Marden. I'd also learn the grading software in the cold store, since that's the bit of the job that's going to computers anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. Not for my hands, for the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if the fruit price drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Cobb cuts hours first, he did it two years ago. Last time we lost about a hundred and fifty a month and Leila took a fourth day at the salon. We'd have to cut Sami's football club, and he's the goalkeeper, so that's a real conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a new AI job you could see yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something checking the computer's decisions in a packhouse, if they need someone who knows fruit. I'm not a tech person, but I know a bruised Comice when I see one. If it's proven and someone's done it first, I'd try.

S2.say: I'd say politicians should stop shouting and do something sensible, like retraining. Some will lose out and some will do well, and it needs managing.
S2.think: The bigger worry is the supermarket buyers becoming computers that are harder to haggle with. That would squeeze the fruit price, and the price squeezes us.
S2.do: Asks Mr Cobb how next year's fruit price looks and, if it's falling, looks for winter evening shifts at a warehouse. Learns the cold store's grading software.
S2.feel: A bit anxious, not about his hands but about the price.
S2.quote: Computers might be harder to haggle with. That would squeeze the price, and the price squeezes us.
S2.fieldNote: He traced the office change to his own pay through a chain of steps: buyers, price, hours. He'd try a new AI-related job only once someone else had proven it, which is classic for him. Cutting his son's football club was the real cost he named.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a fair deal, maybe a tax on the big winners to help people who lose out. I'm not for tearing everything down, but this would be too much at once. I'd vote for whoever has the calmest plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel lucky, which is strange. My hands are worth something in that picture. But if Leila's customers are office people who lose their jobs, they'll cut their own hair, and her three days become two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Cobb for a few more hours, since physical work matters more now. I'd tell Leila to build up the older customers, the ones on pensions, they keep coming. And I'd fix our mortgage rate if the bank would let us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for us, worried for friends. A strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Raj from the juice factory retrained as a bookkeeper after it closed. He did everything right, evening classes, the lot. In this picture, he loses his second job too, and I don't know what I'd say to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Raj, if you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come to Cobb's and I'll teach you to prune, badly. He'd laugh. Then I'd ask Mr Cobb, because I'd mean it.

S3.say: I'd say we need a fair deal, maybe a tax on the big winners to help those who lose. I'm not for tearing things down, but this would be too much at once.
S3.think: I'd feel lucky, because my hands are worth something in that picture. But Leila's office customers might lose their jobs and start cutting their own hair.
S3.do: Asks Mr Cobb for more hours and encourages Leila to build up pensioner customers. Asks the bank about fixing the mortgage rate.
S3.feel: A strange mix: uneasy for his family, worried for friends.
S3.quote: He did everything right, evening classes, the lot. In this picture, he loses his second job too
S3.fieldNote: His mood held steady while his worry shifted to his friend Raj, who retrained into bookkeeping after the same factory closed. The idea that doing everything right might not be enough clearly troubled him. He'd vote for the calmest plan, not the loudest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, a slow rollout, and help for people while they switch. I wouldn't say ban them, that never works. But you can't just turn people off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, orchards are already trialling picking robots, with suction arms, I've seen a video from a farm two counties over. Pruning will take them longer, but grading and cold store work go first. I think I'd lose half my hours in two years, maybe all of it in four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be the one who looks after the robots on Cobb's, if he buys them, since I'll have seen others doing it first. I'd use the AI tools more, to learn the basics. And I'd sit down with Leila and work out what we can lose, the car, the football, before the bank decides for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd spent years learning a skill that a machine learns in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dennis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis is sixty-one, he'd say he'll retire before they get the pruning right. Maybe he would. But I'm forty-three with a mortgage, I can't retire out of the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the trees will still need someone who loves them, and that I'm going to try to be that person. Nadia would ask if the robot can come for tea. Sami would just want to know about the football.

S4.say: I'd say we need rules, a slow rollout and help for people while they switch. Banning never works, but you can't just turn people off.
S4.think: Orchards are already trialling picking robots, I've seen it. Grading and the cold store go first, and I think I'd lose half my hours in two years, maybe all of it in four.
S4.do: Asks to look after any robots Mr Cobb buys and uses AI tools to learn the basics. Sits down with Leila to plan cuts like the car and football before the bank forces them.
S4.feel: Alarmed. Years spent learning a skill a machine could learn in a month.
S4.quote: I'm forty-three with a mortgage, I can't retire out of the way.
S4.fieldNote: The robot card turned him from calm reasoning to alarm, though he stayed measured in how he spoke. His contrast with the head man, who could simply retire, was the clearest line of the interview. He'd still try to run the robots, but only after seeing others do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots. What would help is a gradual plan everyone knows in advance, and help with the mortgage for a year if you lose hours. A year is enough time to learn something, not enough if you're also panicking about the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the trees. A Bramley tree lives sixty, seventy years. Some of the ones I prune were planted before I was born, and they'll be there after the robots. I find that quite calming, honestly.

headlineQuote: I'm forty-three with a mortgage, I can't retire out of the way.
portrait: Omar Zhang is 43, in his third winter at an apple and pear orchard after sixteen years on a juice factory bottling line that moved abroad. He's married to Leila, who cuts hair three days a week, and they have two children, a mortgage and little saved. He weighs both sides of everything and uses AI now and then, trusting it only after it got a pear disease wrong. He stays calm through the early scenarios, traces office change to fruit prices and his hours, and becomes alarmed when picking and grading robots arrive, knowing he can't retire out of the way like the older head man.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because grading and picking go first and he could lose half his hours in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A gradual plan everyone knows in advance, and a year of help with the mortgage if hours are lost, so there's time to learn something new.
